subtopics.title: Why City Air Differs from Farm Air

questions.question: Urban surfaces like tar and concrete are described as low-albedo because they:
options: Reflect little radiation and absorb most of it, storing heat
Reflect nearly all radiation back to space
Cannot be heated by the sun
Evaporate water quickly

questions.question: Urban relative humidity runs lower than rural humidity mainly because:
options: City air is always colder
Rain is piped away by storm-water drains and vegetation is paved over, leaving little water to evaporate
Cities receive no rainfall
Farms irrigate the air directly

questions.question: Wind in a city is best described as:
options: Uniformly stronger than over farmland
Completely absent
Slower on average, but squeezed into gusty funnels between tall buildings
Always blowing toward the city centre

questions.question: Cities are slightly cloudier and wetter than their surroundings because:
options: Cities are always beside the sea
Storm-water drains evaporate huge volumes
Buildings physically block rain from leaving
Heat-island convection lifts air, and urban particles act as abundant condensation nuclei

subtopics.title: The Urban Heat Island — Definition and Causes

questions.question: The urban heat island is strongest:
options: At night and in winter, peaking over the dense city centre
At midday in summer, over the suburbs
At dawn over the rural fringe
Only during heat waves

questions.question: The dips in the heat-island temperature profile occur over:
options: The central business district
Parks and open water, proving that vegetation and moisture cool
Industrial areas
Highways

questions.question: The urban canyon contributes to the heat island because:
options: Wind cannot enter a city at all
Canyons channel cold air into the streets
Walls trap radiation, bouncing it into the street, and the narrow sky-view lets streets radiate away little heat at night
Buildings generate their own sunlight

questions.question: Anthropogenic heat strengthens the island in winter because:
options: The sun is closer in winter
Vegetation grows faster in winter
Rain falls harder in winter
Heating systems, fires and engines release the most waste heat exactly when heating demand peaks

subtopics.title: Heat Island Effects and How Cities Cool Themselves

questions.question: Hot city nights during heat waves are dangerous chiefly because:
options: The body is denied its overnight recovery period, raising heat-stress illness and death
Streetlights fail in the heat
Rain becomes more acidic at night
Wind stops completely at night

questions.question: In South African cities, the residents hit hardest by the heat island are:
options: People in air-conditioned offices
Families under corrugated-iron roofs in informal settlements
Motorists on highways
People living beside parks

questions.question: A street tree cools the city twice because it:
options: Blocks wind and reflects streetlight
Absorbs carbon and releases oxygen
Shades the surface below it and transpires, spending solar energy on evaporation
Lowers humidity and raises albedo

questions.question: Which pairing of strategy and cause is correct?
options: Light-coloured roofs — attacks the urban canyon
Permeable paving — attacks anthropogenic heat
Public transport — attacks the sealed ground
Retention ponds and wetlands — attack the missing evaporation by keeping water in the city

subtopics.title: The Pollution Dome and the Pollution Plume

questions.question: The one-line distinction between dome and plume is:
options: The same urban pollution takes a dome shape in calm weather and streams out as a plume when the wind blows
The dome is factory smoke and the plume is vehicle exhaust
Domes occur in summer and plumes in spring
The plume forms first and becomes a dome later

questions.question: Rising smoke flattens out beneath a winter inversion because:
options: The wind above pushes it back down
It climbs only while warmer than its surroundings, and the warm inversion layer removes its buoyancy
Smoke is heavier than all air
Cold air above sucks it sideways

questions.question: The environmental-justice point about the pollution dome is that:
options: All suburbs are affected identically
Only industry suffers from its own smoke
The dome is thickest where poor households must burn coal and wood for warmth, so they breathe the worst air
The dome only affects the countryside

questions.question: Which is a weather-wise (rather than source-cutting) strategy against the dome?
options: Fitting scrubbers to factory stacks
Electrifying households
Tightening vehicle emission standards
Banning open burning on stable winter days when the inversion lid is down

subtopics.title: The City Is a Storage Heater

questions.question: The warm face-brick wall an hour after sunset demonstrates that urban materials:
options: Store the day's radiation and release it slowly at night
Generate their own heat chemically
Cool faster than farm soil
Reflect all sunlight away

questions.question: The city 'cannot sweat' because:
options: Urban air is too dry for sweating
Its rain is drained away and its vegetation removed, leaving almost nothing to evaporate
Concrete produces water vapour
The heat island prevents all rainfall

questions.question: In the stairwell picture of the urban canyon, the bouncing ball stands for:
options: Rainwater running down the walls
Wind gusting between towers
Radiation reflected wall to wall and trapped in the street
Sound echoing between buildings

subtopics.title: Cooling the Island — Undo Each Cause

questions.question: The parking-bay principle — the white car is touchable after a January afternoon, the black one is not — justifies which strategy?
options: Light-coloured roofs and paving to raise albedo
Planting more trees
Permeable paving
Building wind corridors

questions.question: 'Reinstalling the city's sweat glands' means:
options: Installing more air conditioners
Street trees, parks and roof gardens that shade surfaces and transpire
Painting the roofs white
Widening the storm-water drains

questions.question: The evidence in the temperature profile that greening works is:
options: The peak over the CBD
The rise across the suburbs
The dip in the line over every large park
The fall at the rural fringe

questions.question: The why-it-matters sentence for the strategy essay says cooling a city is:
options: Only about comfort on warm evenings
Impossible in developing countries
A matter for rural municipalities
Health policy, justice policy and energy policy in one, because heat kills selectively and strains the grid

questions.question: In the pot picture, the lid over the winter city is:
options: The temperature inversion — warm air lying over the cold surface air
The cloud layer of a cold front
The pollution plume
The heat island itself

questions.question: Calm weather builds a dome; wind builds a:
options: Second dome
Plume — the same smoke drawn out downwind as a dirty streamer
Thunderstorm
Sea breeze

questions.question: Winter clinics inside the dome fill with respiratory cases mainly because:
options: Cold air alone causes asthma
The dome blocks all sunlight
Coal and wood smoke pools under the inversion exactly where households must burn fuel for warmth
The plume carries pollen into town

questions.question: Since the winter inversion cannot be removed, the strategies aim to:
options: Blow the lid away with fans
Heat the city until the inversion breaks
Move the city to the coast
Make less smoke and time it wisely — clean energy, filtered stacks, no burning on still days, industry zoned downwind
